# What this book establishes {.unnumbered}

This book reports a research program on **surrogates for steady,
boundary-driven, three-dimensional PDE problems**: given a discretized
boundary (a mesh of cells with positions, normals, measures and whatever
data the boundary conditions carry) and the problem's global inputs, zero
or more global vector inputs (a body-force direction, an applied field) and
zero or more global scalar inputs (a thermal diffusivity, a viscosity, an
isotropic Young's modulus, a Reynolds number), predict the steady field on
that boundary and in the domain it bounds. Every experiment in this book
instantiates that class on external aerodynamics, where the boundary is a
vehicle or a wing, the single global vector input is the freestream
direction and there is no global scalar input; that instance is the test bed, not the definition of the
problem. The program built an architecture, ISLA (Invariant Slice
Attention; the code class is `ISLA`),^[Pronounced "eye-la"; an *isla* is an
island, a shape defined entirely by its boundary. An earlier exact-kernel
design of this program is documented in the repository's `book/archive/`
directory, outside this book.] and measured it against GeoTransolver and
Transolver under one frozen, parameter- and token-matched protocol on two
production aerodynamics datasets (DrivAerML, HiLiftAeroML). The audience is
applied mathematicians and machine-learning researchers; every term is defined
at first use and every number is computed live from a checked-in artifact.

ISLA has one reference configuration: the frame-free relative frame with the
total-measure length scale (`frame_mode="relative"`,
`scale_mode="total_measure"`, the class default). Two documented variants
appear where a number comes from them and are named each time: the
constant-gauge variant (plain-mean centre, constant reference length) and the
similarity-gauge variant (Horvitz–Thompson centroid, RMS radius). Every ratio
between architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error, so a value
above one favours ISLA; every error is the cell-area-weighted relative L2 of
@sec-metrics, scored in float32.

## The verdict {#sec-verdict}

**ISLA has no measured accuracy advantage over GeoTransolver or plain
Transolver on the surface task when every model receives the freestream at
the same unit scale: the baselines lead on every HiLiftAeroML rung measured
and on DrivAerML at the reference size. What ISLA contributes is a set of
exact contracts that earn a 6% and 19% accuracy lead over augmented baselines
when geometries arrive in arbitrary poses, a sampling-consistent frame that
degrades 1.2x under a 10:1 sampling-density bias where every configuration
centred on the sampled points degrades 10–16x, and an interior configuration
that leads GeoTransolver-volume on interior velocity (1.37x) and trails on
pressure (0.93x) and eddy viscosity (0.87x).** That sentence is the whole
book, and every chapter either supports one clause of it or bounds it.

The protocol item that decides the surface comparison. Fed the physical
freestream velocity (2,679.5 in/s on HiLiftAeroML), GeoTransolver's
global-context projector collapses to one occupied slice, and both baselines
lose 3.4–3.8x at 35 training cases against the same models fed the unit
direction; the protocol therefore requires the unit direction for every
architecture (@sec-part-baseline). Under that rule, at 35 HiLiftAeroML
training cases GeoTransolver reaches a surface-pressure error of 0.111 (best
learning rate; 0.124 at 1e-3) and Transolver 0.115, against ISLA's reference
configuration at 0.1529 and its constant-gauge variant at 0.1377: GeoTransolver
is 0.73x of the reference and 0.80x of the variant, Transolver 0.75x and
0.83x (three seeds each; @sec-de-result). ISLA's weights-off ablation
reaches 0.1225; it reads the mesh density and is measured but not adopted
(@sec-principle).

What stands on the surface. On every HiLiftAeroML rung with unit-direction
baselines (GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the freestream as a unit
direction, matching ISLA's input; named udrv in the artifacts) the baselines
are ahead: at 210 cases GeoTransolver is 0.84x of
the constant-gauge variant and 0.75x of the reference, Transolver 0.90x and
0.81x; at 510 cases 0.84x and 0.90x of the constant-gauge variant (the
reference is not yet measured there); at 4 never-seen training geometries
GeoTransolver is 0.76x of the variant and 0.75x of the reference, even by
geometry (9 of 18 each way); at 21 geometries 0.92x and 0.88x, Transolver
0.93x and 0.88x; at the fixed angle 0.78x and 0.68x, Transolver 0.86x and
0.75x, on 18 of 18 held-out geometries; the 1,260-case rung is not yet
measured with unit-direction baselines (@sec-data-efficiency,
@sec-program-status). On DrivAerML at 435 cars GeoTransolver reaches 0.0503
and Transolver 0.0517 against the reference's 0.0552 (0.91x and 0.94x) and the
constant-gauge variant's 0.0557; the measure-weighted research variants of the
baselines reach 0.0498 and 0.0522; below full data GeoTransolver leads by
1.2–1.3x (@sec-full-data). At 512 width and 80,000 cells the baselines and
ISLA's constant-gauge variant are within 3% (GeoTransolver 0.0419,
constant-gauge variant 0.0428, Transolver 0.0431; the similarity-gauge variant
0.0431 at the same cost), and the reference configuration, which trains there
only at the width learning rate 3.75e-4, reaches 0.0442 (1.05x GeoTransolver;
@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict), so half of the reference-size deficit is a
statement about that size and resolution and the remaining 5% is the reference
frame's price at scale, not the rate's: the constant-gauge variant retrained at
the same 3.75e-4 scores 0.0424 (@sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict). The reference frame's price
against the constant-gauge variant is 0% on DrivAerML, 1–5% on the
never-seen-geometry count rungs, 11% where validation geometries recur in
training (35 and 210 cases), 14.5% at the fixed angle and 3% at the
512 × 80k corner (4% at a matched learning rate; @sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict); on
both splits
tested with an exact full-geometry frame the price is the plain mean's mesher
pattern, not positional information (@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict,
@sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict, @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict).
Across an angle-of-attack or stall boundary every architecture tested loses
about a factor of ten, so coverage, not architecture, governs that axis
(@sec-regime-extrapolation).

What ISLA adds: contracts, consistency, an interior configuration, and a
cost within reach of the baselines. Rotation and translation covariance are
exact by algebraic construction (the finite-precision residual of the bf16
training path is a measured quantity, @sec-mt2-contracts); when every
DrivAerML car arrives in a random pose ISLA scores 0.0566 (1.01x its
in-pose error) against GeoTransolver with SO(3) augmentation at 0.0602
(1.20x its in-pose error) and Transolver with augmentation at 0.0676 (1.31x):
6% and 19% ahead (@sec-pose, @sec-scoreboard-pose). Training is stable
across a decade of learning rate where GeoTransolver degrades 4–14x
(@sec-robustness-lr). Consistency: under a 10:1 sampling-density bias with
the frame taken from the biased sample, the reference frame degrades 1.2x,
where the constant-gauge variant, the released GeoTransolver and Transolver
(12x each) and their measure-weighted variants (14–16x) all centre on the
sampled points and collapse; under refinement the measure-weighted ISLA's
convention-swap penalty converges 2.9x → 1.45x → 1.05x from 2,500 to 40,000
cells while the released baselines stay at 3–7x (@sec-consistency-bench,
@tbl-consistency-matrix, @sec-nb-mw-postcenter, @sec-nb-mix-refinement).
The Horvitz–Thompson-centred, measure-weighted baselines that match ISLA on
consistency are research variants that locate the property; the released
GeoTransolver and Transolver are not modified
(@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines). Measure weights are a correctness
requirement: their in-distribution price on the wings is estimator variance,
which shrinks with cell count, plus mesh-pattern content, which does not and
which collapses under area-proportional sampling to errors worse than
predicting zero; weights-off is an ablation only (@sec-nb-bench-verdict,
@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe).

On the interior task (DrivAerML, 48 validation cars, 10,000 queries), with
its queries admitted as interacting tokens and given the signed distance to
the wall, ISLA's reference configuration at 8.9M parameters scores 0.0550 on
interior pressure, 0.0782 on velocity and 0.1005 on eddy viscosity against
unit-direction GeoTransolver-volume's 0.0513, 0.1070 and 0.0879 at 27.6M
parameters: GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA 0.93, 1.37 and 0.87 (@sec-interior,
@sec-nb-relint-verdict). The similarity-gauge interior variant scores 0.0550
/ 0.0789 / 0.1142 with a 10,000-cell boundary and 0.0553 / 0.0804 / 0.1109
with a 365-cell boundary (three seeds); at matched parameters (27.6M) that
variant leads on pressure by 3% and velocity by 32% and trails on eddy
viscosity by 18%. The interacting decode's prediction depends on the joint
query set, so the model is deployed at its training query count
(@sec-interior-companion, @sec-nb-qcount-verdict); far-wake oversampling at
training makes every field worse (@sec-nb-farwake-verdict). A single-case
study locates the mechanisms: the surface deficit and the interior
eddy-viscosity deficit are capacity, the interior velocity lead is capacity,
and the interior pressure lead of the similarity-gauge variant at full data is
generalization across cars (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict, @sec-nb-overfit-interior).
The passive, query-independent decode is 3.1x behind on interior pressure.
Cost, on one GB300 in bfloat16 at 10,000 tokens and batch 1, both models
compiled as the recipe runs them: ISLA's step is 47 ms at 1.30 GiB with the
geometry recompute on (1.05x GeoTransolver's 45 ms at 2.70 GiB) and 39 ms at
1.94 GiB without (0.86x); at 40,000 tokens the default compiled ISLA takes
119 ms against GeoTransolver's 53 ms (2.2x), and the exact fused geometry
kernel (opt-in, `geo_kernel="fused"`) takes 52 ms at 4.5 GiB against 10.0 GiB.
Every stage but the MLP is memory-bound; the relational invariants carry 61%
of the traffic (@sec-cost, @sec-nb-kernel-study).

: The standing of ISLA against GeoTransolver and Transolver in every setting
measured, as baseline error divided by ISLA error where a ratio is given
(above one favours ISLA). Ratios name the ISLA configuration they divide by:
the reference configuration (relative frame, total-measure scale) or the
constant-gauge variant; "unit-direction" means the baseline received the freestream
as a unit direction, the protocol's requirement. Every density ratio states
its frame. Each row's protocol, seeds, statistics and artifact are in the
chapter that owns it: @sec-scoreboard (every row on one page),
@sec-data-efficiency (HiLift rows), @sec-full-data (DrivAerML surface, regime
extrapolation, pose, contracts), @sec-interior (interior rows). {#tbl-verdict}

## The result in one picture

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   HiLiftAeroML surface pressure error against training cases under the
#|   unit-direction protocol. Relative L2 error of surface pressure (cell-area
#|   weighted, float32) on the shared 180-case validation set for unit-direction
#|   GeoTransolver (red circles), unit-direction Transolver (grey triangles,
#|   dashed), the ISLA reference configuration (blue filled squares; relative
#|   frame, total-measure scale; trained at 35 and 210 cases) and the ISLA
#|   constant-gauge variant (blue open squares, dotted; all four rungs). Lines
#|   join seed means; bands span the seeds; the factors are each baseline's
#|   seed mean divided by the constant-gauge variant's (above one would favour
#|   ISLA). How to read this: both baselines sit below both ISLA
#|   configurations at every rung measured. It does not show the 1,260-case
#|   rung for the baselines or the reference (not yet measured,
#|   @sec-program-status), nor the never-seen-geometry and fixed-angle splits
#|   (@tbl-verdict). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500
#|   epochs, bfloat16 training, no augmentation, each architecture at its
#|   declared learning rate (GeoTransolver 3e-3 at 35 cases and 1e-3 above,
#|   Transolver 3e-3, ISLA 1e-3), two or three seeds per point, final-epoch
#|   checkpoints. Data: results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json,
#|   results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
#|   results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json,
#|   results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json,
#|   results/relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json,
#|   results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json.
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
fpall = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
u210 = J("udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json")
u510 = J("udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json")
rf = J("relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json")["hilift_val"]
ff = J("frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json")["hilift_val"]
fp = lambda runs, keys: [runs[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
a210 = u210["three_seed_addendum_fp32"]
series = {
    "gt": {35: fp(fp35, [f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)]),
           210: a210["gt_unit_lr1e3"]["seed_pressure"],
           510: u510["arms_fp32"]["gt_unit"]["seed_pressure"]},
    "t": {35: fp(fp35, [f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]),
          210: a210["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"],
          510: u510["arms_fp32"]["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["seed_pressure"]},
    "isla_cg": {35: fp(fp35, [f"lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]),
                210: u210["arms_fp32"]["isla"]["seed_pressure"],
                510: u510["arms_fp32"]["isla_prior"]["seed_pressure"],
                1260: fp(fpall, [f"mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])},
    "isla_ref": {35: [rf[f"rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)],
                 210: [ff[f"rf_hl_mt2_meas_scarce_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]},
}
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver (unit direction)", "o", "-", "full"),
         "t": (GREY, "Transolver (unit direction)", "^", "--", "full"),
         "isla_cg": (BLUE, "ISLA, constant-gauge variant", "s", ":", "none"),
         "isla_ref": (BLUE, "ISLA, reference configuration", "s", "-", "full")}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.0))
for key in ("isla_ref", "isla_cg", "gt", "t"):
    c, name, mk, ls, fill = style[key]
    xs = sorted(series[key]); ms_ = [statistics.mean(series[key][x]) for x in xs]
    lo = [min(series[key][x]) for x in xs]; hi = [max(series[key][x]) for x in xs]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, ms_, color=c, lw=2.0, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3, label=name,
            mfc=(c if fill == "full" else "white"), mec=c, mew=1.8)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9, handlelength=2.6)
lines = ["baseline ÷ ISLA constant-gauge variant (seed means)"]
for x in (35, 210, 510):
    ref = statistics.mean(series["isla_cg"][x])
    r_gt = statistics.mean(series["gt"][x]) / ref; r_t = statistics.mean(series["t"][x]) / ref
    lines.append(f"{x:,} cases: GeoTransolver {r_gt:.2f}x, Transolver {r_t:.2f}x")
lines.append("1,260 cases: baselines and reference not yet measured")
ax.text(0.985, 0.03, "\n".join(lines), transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom",
        fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, linespacing=1.4,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec=BASELINE))
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 510, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "510", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.15]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.03", "0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.15"])
ax.set_ylim(0.025, 0.19); ax.set_xlim(25, 4200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, area-weighted relative L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("HiLiftAeroML surface pressure against training cases, unit-direction protocol, float32",
             color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## How to read this book

Part I defines the problem, the datasets and splits, the metrics and the
protocol (@sec-problem), then the architecture, ISLA
(@sec-mt2), and the baselines with the fair-comparison rules
(@sec-baselines). Part II is the evidence on production aerodynamics. It
opens with the scoreboard (@sec-scoreboard): every cross-architecture
measurement of the book, surface, interior, pose, consistency and cost, on
one page with matched inputs and one instrument, for a reader who needs the
standing and not the derivation. The chapters behind it are data
efficiency (@sec-data-efficiency); accuracy at full data, the robustness
contracts and regime extrapolation (@sec-full-data,
@sec-regime-extrapolation); and boundary-to-interior prediction
(@sec-interior), which also answers why the architecture does not evaluate
exact boundary-integral kernels (@sec-interior-negatives). Part III
states the limits of every claim and the experiments that would move them
(@sec-limits) and holds the live status ledger of the program
(@sec-program-status). Two appendices follow. The first
(@sec-principled-decisions) is the ledger of design decisions: for every
place where a rejected alternative would have scored better on the
in-distribution metric, what it would have bought, what it read that the
physics does not provide, and the evidence, together with the principle
that decided it; it is written for the paper's "why". The second is the
dated lab notebook (@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and
verdict, including the failed ones, in the order they happened.

Three habits of this book: a comparison is only reported when parameters,
tokens per case, epochs, peak memory and the scale of every input are
matched or the mismatch is stated in the same sentence, and every ratio between architectures is written
as baseline error divided by ISLA error, so a value above one favours ISLA; a claim is only reported with the split it was
measured on and the statistic behind it; and a limit is stated next to the
claim it limits, not in a separate place.

## What this book does not claim

It does not claim that ISLA is more accurate than GeoTransolver or plain
Transolver anywhere on the surface task. Under the unit-direction protocol the
baselines are 0.68–0.95x of ISLA's reference configuration on every
HiLiftAeroML and DrivAerML rung measured (the 1,260-case rung against the
constant-gauge variant only), and at 512 width and 80,000 cells the baselines and the
constant-gauge variant are within 3% while the reference configuration,
trained at the width learning rate, is 1.05x GeoTransolver (@tbl-verdict). Comparisons against
baselines fed the physical freestream velocity measure the protocol's input
scale, not the architectures, and appear only as such (@sec-part-baseline).
The HiLift accuracy figures are validation-set figures (final-epoch
checkpoints, no checkpoint selection; the sealed test was spent on regime
extrapolation, and because those regime test sets cover all 180 geometries,
every remaining HiLiftAeroML split is held out per checkpoint but is not an
independent program-level confirmation, @sec-limits-validation). The interior
lead is on velocity only and is conditional: it requires at least the training
count of points to be queried together (@sec-interior-companion), and pressure
and eddy viscosity trail GeoTransolver-volume at the reference parameter count
(@sec-interior). ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract, not an
in-distribution accuracy edge on vehicle data: GeoTransolver trained in a
canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1% cost (@sec-pose), and the 6%
and 19% lead is measured against baselines that learn pose from augmentation,
in random poses only. Sampling consistency is a fine-mesh-limit property, not
invariance: the reference frame's 1.2x under a 10:1 bias is a 10,000-cell
statement, and at the fixed angle the bias bar is not yet met at 40,000 cells
(@sec-robustness-density, @sec-consistency-bench). Cost parity with
GeoTransolver holds at 10,000 tokens on the compiled path; at 40,000 tokens
the default path is 2.2x and parity needs the opt-in fused kernel (@sec-cost).
Neither architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary, and neither
transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle family (@sec-regime-extrapolation,
@sec-full-data).
